extracted.intended_audience: card issuers, industry stakeholders, consumer advocates, and legal/regulatory professionals participating in CFPB rulemaking or notice-and-comment on credit card late fee safe harbors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidentiary criteria the CFPB uses to determine an appropriate safe-harbor late fee amount for larger card issuers, focusing on deterrence, costs, consumer conduct, and empirical evidence. Applies to rulemaking analysis of first and subsequent late-payment fees (including six-billing-cycle distinctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterrent effect of late fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A late fee of any dollar amount has some deterrent effect that is more than no late fee at all; generally a lower late fee amount has less theoretical deterrence than a higher amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB accepts that $8 would have a lesser deterrent effect than current amounts but rejects that deterrence requires setting a safe harbor amount that will have the maximum theoretical deterrence effect. Consider deterrence together with other factors (costs, consumer conduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of late fee to minimum payment amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the safe-harbor late fee amount to typical minimum payment amounts on accounts (e.g., median minimum payment ~ $39–$100 in Y-14 data) to assess the relative cost to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to calculate effective APRs incurred by borrowing a minimum payment for a period (examples: $8 late fee on $100 for one month ≈ 96% APR; $8 on $40 for 10 days ≈ 730% APR), informing whether the fee provides meaningful deterrence for consumers who pay attention to penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Y-14 account-level data
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on Y-14 data from Larger Card Issuers (various years including 2019 and Oct 2021–Sep 2022) to analyze incidence and timing of late payments and how changes in late fee amounts relate to behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Y-14 data provide a richer evidence base than earlier data; CFPB used these data for several analyses including the seventh-month discontinuity test and descriptive statistics on time-to-repayment (within 5, 15, 30 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh-month discontinuity statistical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate whether there is a discontinuous jump in late payments in the seventh month after the last late payment, isolating the potential impact of a lower late fee applicable in month seven compared to months 1–6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analysis focuses on a plausible natural experiment to avoid confounding; CFPB's random subsample from 2019 Y-14 data did not find an effect at conventional confidence levels. Interpretation contingent on consumers understanding issuer fee schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of other consequences of late payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for non-fee consequences that affect consumers' decisions to pay on time, including loss of grace period, increased interest/penalty APRs, and credit-reporting consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The total cost of a late payment is higher than just the late fee; these other consequences can be similar or greater deterrents (especially for transactors who lose a grace period). CFPB incorporates these when evaluating whether a reduced safe harbor will meaningfully affect behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer conduct metrics (time-to-repayment and repeat violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate empirical measures of consumer conduct such as percent of accounts paying within 5/15/30 days and rates of repeat late payments within six billing cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB estimated that a third paid within 5 days, half within 15, and three of five within 30 days; industry Metro 2 reporting does not consider payments late until 30+ days, which factors into risk-management assessments of 'serious' conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness and proportionality balancing (deterrence, cost, consumer conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set safe-harbor amounts by balancing deterrence, the costs to issuers of collecting charges, and observed consumer conduct to ensure fees are reasonable and proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB frames $8 as striking an appropriate balance—still deterring some consumers while reducing excessive fees—and treats statutory factors as guidance rather than strictly controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether fee exceeds issuer costs (covering pre-charge-off collection costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the safe-harbor fee covers pre-charge-off collection costs for the average issuer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB determines the $8 safe harbor will cover pre-charge-off collection costs for the average Larger Card Issuer, consistent with CARD Act requirements and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneous effects and subpopulation impacts (e.g., subprime borrowers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider that different consumer groups may be affected differently (for example, subprime cardholders disproportionately pay late fees and may use late-fee funds toward payments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB recognizes lowering fees may benefit some constrained cardholders by freeing funds for repayment, and evidence (e.g., Grodzicki) suggests decreased late fees increased repayment among subprime in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and relevance of submitted empirical studies and surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate external studies and industry-submitted surveys for confounding, timeframe issues, hypothetical framing, lack of counterfactuals, sample size, and applicability to the rule change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB critiques studies that compare periods affected by the Great Recession or lack control groups, notes surveys' hypothetical nature and missing context (e.g., respondents not told about other late-payment consequences), and prefers evidence about actual late-fee incidence/effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on inapt proxies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on proxies like returned-check penalties, utility bill late fees, or student loan late fees as substitutes for credit card late fee behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such proxies lack comparable financial consequences (e.g., grace period loss, interest accrual, credit reporting) and thus are inapt for deterrence analysis of credit card late fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of issuer non-fee deterrence tools and market changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for other methods issuers use to deter late payments (automatic payments, reminders, well-chosen due dates, repricing/penalty rates, reducing credit lines, limiting rewards, reporting to credit bureaus) and increasing digital enrollment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB notes growth in autopay/online behavior and free consumer access to real-time credit scores enhances non-fee deterrence; issuers may adopt alternative, potentially more efficient practices if late-fee revenue falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: International and historical comparisons (e.g., UK OFT and prior Board rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider international examples and prior regulatory actions (Board's 2010 Final Rule, UK OFT £12 limit) as informative but not determinative due to contextual differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB considered OFT's 2006 limit and subsequent UK studies; cautions about confounding variables and contextual differences (economic conditions, market response) when interpreting such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability and statistical power to observe behavior changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether available data and analysis methods can detect meaningful changes in late-payment prevalence attributable to fee changes (e.g., whether some issuers' varied use of higher safe harbor allows detection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB notes its analysis does not depend on all issuers charging particular amounts; as long as some used higher safe harbor, the data should detect changes, but detectability depends on consumers' awareness and statistical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of industry-provided descriptive data on reoffending
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrutinize industry claims about reduced recurrence after fee assessment by requiring comparisons to counterfactuals (e.g., what would happen under $8 vs current fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB finds disclosed industry statistics insufficient because they do not show effects against the counterfactual of a lower fee; descriptive declines in subsequent delinquency are consistent with many explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of potential issuer responses and second-order effects (interest rates, pricing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate that issuers may offset lost late-fee revenue by raising interest rates or changing pricing/risk-management, which could alter deterrence and distributional outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB notes these responses could indirectly make late payments more costly and that issuers retain risk-based pricing tools and penalty-rate repricing consistent with Regulation Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for evidence of actual incurred-fee effects over hypothetical survey responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight more heavily empirical evidence of consumers' behavior when they actually incur late fees than hypothetical survey responses about deterrence thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB explains surveys asking about hypothetical fee points are limited (lack of context about other consequences, whether respondents had funds/awareness) and therefore less informative than Y-14 and other empirical analyses.
